stem: A 29-year-old woman, six weeks after delivering her first child, has pain on the thumb side of the right wrist when she lifts the baby. The area over the radial styloid is tender and slightly swollen. When she tucks the thumb into her fist and tilts the wrist toward the little finger, she has sharp pain. Sensation in the hand is normal, and a wrist x-ray is normal.
oneliner: 29F + new mother lifting baby + radial wrist pain and swelling + positive Finkelstein test + normal x-ray → next step?
ask: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Surgical release of the first dorsal compartment now
options.C: Carpal tunnel release through a palmar incision
options.D: MRI of the wrist before any treatment
options.E: Long arm cast immobilization for six weeks

whyNot.A: Reserved for **refractory** cases after conservative care and injection
whyNot.C: Her pain is over **radial-side tendons** and **sensation is normal**, so the median nerve is not involved
whyNot.D: Diagnosis is **clinical** and imaging is not needed for a typical case
whyNot.E: Excessive and unneeded; a **thumb spica splint** is enough

answer: Rest with a thumb spica splint and NSAIDs
why: This is **de Quervain tenosynovitis** of the **abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis** in the first dorsal compartment. First-line care is **rest, a thumb spica splint and NSAIDs**; a corticosteroid injection follows if symptoms persist, and **surgical release** is a last resort.

idea.rule: De Quervain is tendon sheath inflammation, so treat with rest and anti-inflammatories first.
also: Common in new mothers and in repetitive thumb use
Involves abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis

stem: A 16-year-old girl has tingling along the inner side of her hand and forearm after carrying a heavy backpack for a while. Symptoms ease when she removes the bag or rests her arm. Pulses are normal. A chest x-ray shows a small extra rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra. Nerve conduction studies are normal.
oneliner: 16F + ulnar-side hand tingling with a heavy backpack + relieved by removing it + normal pulses + cervical rib on x-ray → first-line management?
ask: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Immediate resection of the cervical rib
options.B: Carpal tunnel release of the wrist ligament
options.C: Ulnar nerve transposition at the elbow
options.E: Anterior fusion of the cervical spine

whyNot.A: Surgery is for **refractory or vascular** cases after a trial of therapy
whyNot.B: Her symptoms are **ulnar-side** and not from the median nerve at the wrist
whyNot.C: The ulnar nerve does not supply the **inner forearm**, and her **cervical rib** places the compression above the clavicle
whyNot.E: No **disc or cord disease** is described, and fusion is not indicated

answer: Posture correction, stretching and physical therapy
why: This is **neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome**, with the **lower trunk of the brachial plexus** compressed by a **cervical rib**. First-line treatment is **conservative: posture correction, stretching and physical therapy**; **resection of the rib** is kept for those who fail it.

idea.rule: Thoracic outlet syndrome is treated with posture and exercise before surgery.
also: Neurogenic type is the commonest, with C8 and T1 symptoms
Venous type: arm swelling and effort thrombosis
Arterial type: ischemia from subclavian artery compression
Surgical decompression if conservative care fails

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought in after his mother lifted him by the hand when he fell. He holds the right arm still at his side and refuses to use it. There is no swelling, bruise or deformity, and he does not cry when his shoulder, wrist or the bones of the forearm are pressed.
oneliner: 2M + lifted by the hand + will not use arm + no swelling, bruise or deformity + non-tender bones → next step?
ask: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Obtain an elbow x-ray before any manipulation
options.B: Apply a long arm cast for three weeks
options.C: Supinate the forearm while flexing the elbow
options.D: Refer to orthopedics for open reduction
options.E: Sling the arm for three weeks without reducing it

whyNot.A: Not needed when the **history is typical** and **exam shows no bone tenderness**
whyNot.B: No fracture is suspected, and a cast would **leave the head out of place**
whyNot.D: Closed reduction at the bedside is **simple and effective**; surgery is not required
whyNot.E: A sling alone **does not reduce** the displaced radial head

answer: Closed reduction by supination with elbow flexion (or hyperpronation)
why: With a **typical pulled-arm history, a non-tender bony exam and no swelling**, this is **radial head subluxation**, treated by **closed reduction**: supinate the forearm with flexion, or hyperpronate. **Imaging is only for atypical history or findings**; a click and prompt use of the arm confirm success.

idea.rule: A typical nursemaid elbow is reduced first and imaged only if it fails.
also: Imaging is reserved for a fall, swelling or tenderness
Expect use of the arm within minutes of reduction
Annular ligament matures and thickens with age

stem: A 19-year-old woman who is a gymnast fell on her outstretched left hand during practice. The wrist is mildly swollen and tender in the anatomic snuffbox, and pain increases when she grips. A wrist x-ray in several views shows no fracture.
oneliner: 19F + gymnast + fall on outstretched hand + snuffbox tenderness + normal x-ray → next step?
ask: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Thumb spica splint, then repeat imaging or MRI
options.B: Reassure her and discharge without a splint
options.C: Open reduction and internal fixation of the scaphoid
options.D: Radionuclide bone scan as the first test
options.E: A short course of NSAIDs with return to training

whyNot.B: A normal first film does not **exclude a scaphoid fracture**, which can be occult
whyNot.C: There is **no demonstrated fracture** and no displacement
whyNot.D: A reasonable later alternative, but not the **first** step; splint now
whyNot.E: Sends her back **unprotected** and risks nonunion and avascular necrosis

answer: Immobilize in a thumb spica splint and repeat x-ray in 1 to 2 weeks or get MRI
why: **Snuffbox tenderness** after a fall on an outstretched hand means a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, and the **first x-ray can miss it**. Immobilize in a **thumb spica splint** and either repeat the x-ray in **7 to 14 days** or obtain **MRI**.

idea.rule: Clinical suspicion beats a normal first x-ray in the scaphoid: treat as fractured.
also: MRI is the most sensitive early test
Risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
Snuffbox borders: extensor pollicis longus on one side, abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis on the other
